Vs.

full_judgment:
Bijan Kumar Das, J: This rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 7.11.1999 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and S.C.C. Judge decreeing S.C.C. Suit No. 30 of 1995. 

 4. The trial court framed all the relevant issues and on consideration of the evidence on record came to the finding that the defendant could not produce any paper or rent receipt showing payment of rent for the months of Baishakh and Jaistha, 1402 B.S. The trial court therefore concluded that the defendant is a defaulter and that the plaintiff bonafide requires the suit premises and a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act terminating the tenancy was served on the defendant. Accordingly by judgment and decree dated 7.11.1999 the trial court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. 

 7. Mr. Farid Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 on the other hand, supports the decision of the trial court and submits that the trial court considered the evidence on record and found the defendant a defaulter and committed no error of law in granting a decree for eviction of the defendant from the suit premises. According to the Mr. Ahmed, the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was valid and proper notice which legally determined the tenancy and the trial court has rightly decreed the suit. 

 10. With regard to legality and propriety of the notice 106 of the Transfer of Property Act I have considered the notice exhibit 3 and it appears that the notice was issued by one Shahin Ara Tafader on behalf of Ashoke Kumar Nandi and others and the A/D exhibit 3 'Ka' shows that it was duly served on the defendant. Exhibit 3 and 3 'Ka' clearly show that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was duly served on the defendant and that the notice was issued by the landlord Ashoke Kumar Nandi (plaintiff No. 5) on behalf of all the landlords. Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that the lease of immovably property, other than for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable on the part of either lessor or lessee by 15 day's notice expiring with the end of a. month of the tenancy. This section further provides that every notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act must be in writing signed by or on behalf of the person giving it either he sent by post to the party who is intended to be bound by it. Thus, on is perusal of the provision of law it does not appear that all the lessors are required to issue the notice. Upon a construction of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act I am of the view that any of the lessors, if they are more than one, may issue the notice or anyone representing a lessor may issue a notice terminating the tenancy and non-issuance of the notice by all the lessors, if they are more than one, would not disentitle the landlord to get a decree for ejectment of the tenant. A notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act should be construed liberally and not strictly. In that view of the matter, I find that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was a legal and proper notice and was sufficient to terminate the tenancy between the plaintiffs and the defendant. 

 11. The finding of the trial court that the landlords bonafide require the suit premises cannot be sustained as this finding is based on consideration of no evidence but that will not defeat the plaintiff from getting a decree for ejectment of the defendant from the suit premises when there is a clear finding that the defendant is a defaulter. The plaintiff examined himself as P.W. 1 and one Pran Gopal Nandi was examined as P.W. 2 who was produced to prove the default of the defendant in payment of monthly rent. The defendant examined himself as D.W. 1 and was supported by Paresh Chandra Sarker, D.W. 2. This P.W. 2 was produced to prove payment of rent for the year 1402 B.S. D.W. 1 did not say anything with regard to payment of rent for the month of Baishakh, 1402 B.S. A suggestion was put to him that he is a full brother of the defendant. In any view, on the face of absence of any rent receipt showing payment of rents for the months of Baishakh and Jaistha, 1402 B.S. the defendant must be held to be a defaulter. Having considered all aspect, I do not find any illegality or infirmity in the impugned decision. I do not, therefore, find any merit in this rule. Accordingly this rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 7.11.1999 passed by the 3rd Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka in S.C.C. Suit No. 30 of 1995 is hereby affirmed.
